questions.question: What is JpaRepository and why do you extend it instead of CrudRepository?
questions.title: JpaRepository vs CrudRepository — Why Use JpaRepository
questions.direct_answer: JpaRepository is Spring Data JPA's store-specific repository interface. It combines list-based CRUD with paging and sorting and adds JPA operations such as flush, saveAndFlush, and batch deletion. It is convenient for most JPA repositories, but CrudRepository or a selective base interface can be used when a smaller public API is intentional.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the Spring Data repository hierarchy and the concrete, practical reasons JpaRepository is the production default rather than a vague 'it has more methods'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Extending CrudRepository 'because it's simpler', then converting Iterable to List in every service method and missing flush()/batch operations when they're needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the List-vs-Iterable return type and the JPA-only methods (saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch) as concrete reasons, and note JpaRepository is a strict superset so there's no trade-off

sections.title: Why JpaRepository Is Convenient for JPA
sections.content:
Repository inheritance defines the methods that become part of the data-access API. Extending JpaRepository<Order, Long> gives ordinary CRUD, list results, pagination, sorting, and JPA-specific methods. Extending CrudRepository gives a smaller, store-neutral set and returns Iterable for findAll.

JpaRepository is therefore a convenience default, not a correctness requirement. For an aggregate that should only be loaded and appended, a selective repository may communicate the domain better than exposing deleteAll. For a normal administrative CRUD screen, JpaRepository avoids unnecessary conversion and extra interface composition.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: JpaRepository is JPA-specific; CrudRepository is store-neutral.
JpaRepository returns List for multi-result CRUD methods and supports paging/sorting.
JPA extras include flush and batch-oriented delete methods.
A smaller repository surface can be deliberate; JpaRepository is not mandatory.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Most Spring Data JPA applications extend JpaRepository because it places the common JPA operations in one interface. Service code gets List results, Pageable and Sort support, and explicit flush or batch-delete operations when needed. That convenience should not become a rule that every repository must expose every method. A domain-specific interface can extend Repository or copy selected signatures when callers should not have unrestricted delete or save access. Current Spring Data hierarchy details also matter: the sorting interfaces were separated from CRUD in version 3, while JpaRepository already composes the suitable list variants.

sections.title: Repository Hierarchy at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Repository|~Marker interface|no methods|just enables Spring Data|the root
blue|CrudRepository|~Basic CRUD|save, findById, delete|returns Iterable<T>|minimal surface
emerald|PagingAndSortingRepository|~Adds paging/sort|findAll(Pageable)|findAll(Sort)|extends CrudRepository
violet|JpaRepository|~Full JPA toolkit|flush, saveAndFlush|deleteAllInBatch, returns List<T>|the production default

sections.title: JpaRepository vs CrudRepository
sections.content:
| Aspect | CrudRepository | JpaRepository |
|---|---|---|
| **Return type** | `Iterable<T>` | `List<T>` (directly usable) |
| **Pagination/sorting** | No | Yes (inherited) |
| **Batch ops** | No | `deleteAllInBatch()`, `saveAll()` |
| **Flush control** | No | `flush()`, `saveAndFlush()` |
| **Best for** | Minimal/library API | Everyday Spring Boot apps |

JpaRepository is a strict superset — it has everything CrudRepository has, plus more.

sections.title: CrudRepository — Iterable Forces Conversion
JpaRepository — List Out of the Box
When to Use Which
sections.content: Use **`JpaRepository`** as the default for nearly every Spring Data JPA repository — you get CRUD, paging, sorting, batch operations, and the convenient `List` return type. Use **`CrudRepository`** only when you deliberately want a tiny API surface (a shared module) or a lightweight contract. **`PagingAndSortingRepository`** is rarely chosen directly. In a typical Spring Boot REST API on PostgreSQL, `JpaRepository` covers ~95% of needs without custom code.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing CrudRepository for 'simplicity'** — you then convert `Iterable` to `List` in every service method, which is more code, not less.
- **Missing the JPA-only helpers** — `saveAndFlush()` and `deleteAllInBatch()` aren't available, so bulk deletes load and delete row by row.
- **Assuming there's a trade-off** — `JpaRepository` is a strict superset; defaulting to it costs nothing at runtime.
- **Forgetting it still generates everything** — you never write an implementation; Spring builds the proxy from the method names.

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is JpaRepository and why do you extend it instead of CrudRepository? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.standard_example: An OrderRepository extending JpaRepository in a Spring Boot app

beats.text: Both are Spring Data repository types. CrudRepository gives the basic save, find, and delete methods. JpaRepository extends it and the paging type. So it also adds paging, sorting, and a handy List return type.
Default to JpaRepository for almost every repository. It's a strict superset, so you give up nothing. Drop to CrudRepository only when you want a tiny API, like a shared library.
Call findAll on a CrudRepository and you get an Iterable. So you loop to build a List. The gotcha is that JpaRepository returns a List directly, so that extra step just goes away.

speakable_v2.cap: So make JpaRepository your default and reach for CrudRepository only when small is the point.

questions.question: What is the difference between findAll() and findAll(Sort) in JpaRepository?
questions.title: findAll() vs findAll(Sort) in JpaRepository
questions.direct_answer: findAll() has no defined result order unless the query includes ORDER BY; insertion order must not be assumed. findAll(Sort) asks the database to order by the named entity properties. Database sorting is not automatically faster than Java sorting—indexes, result size, memory, pagination, and the query plan matter—but it is required when ordering must happen before paging.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you push sorting to the database (ORDER BY) instead of loading all rows and sorting in memory, and whether you know how to express multi-field and directional sorts
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling findAll().stream().sorted(...) which loads the whole table into memory and fails to scale once the table grows
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention multi-field sorting, Sort.Direction.DESC, ignoreCase(), combining with PageRequest, and the need for an index on sorted columns

sections.title: findAll With and Without an Explicit Sort
sections.content:
Relational tables do not preserve a presentation order. A sequence or clustered layout can make one order appear repeatedly during testing, but statistics, plans, vacuuming, and parallel execution can change it. Only ORDER BY creates a result-order contract.

For a small already-loaded collection, Java sorting can be fine. For repository pagination or filtering, put the sort in the query. Validate property names early and keep allowed API sort fields on an allow-list so clients cannot request expensive or unintended expressions.

**Example.** repository.findAll() returns all rows with no guaranteed order. repository.findAll(Sort.by(DESC, "createdAt")) requests a defined order, but a large table should normally use PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by(DESC, "createdAt")) instead of loading everything.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: No ORDER BY means no guaranteed row order.
Sort uses entity property names and becomes an ORDER BY expression.
Add a unique tie-breaker when stable paging matters.
Inspect indexes and the plan instead of assuming every sort is index-backed.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
repository.findAll() can return rows in any order the database chooses. repository.findAll(Sort.by("name").ascending().and(Sort.by("id"))) requests a stable name-then-id order. The id tie-breaker matters when several rows share a name. Sorting in the database is the correct semantic choice for pagination because sorting a single Java page cannot establish the order of rows that were not fetched. An index may help, but the optimizer can still choose an explicit sort.

For example, findAll() is acceptable for a tiny fixed lookup table. For an orders screen, I would request PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending()) so ordering is explicit and memory use is bounded.

sections.title: Sorting Options at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|findAll()|~No ORDER BY|DB-dependent order|not guaranteed|use only for tiny/unordered sets
blue|findAll(Sort)|~Adds ORDER BY|DB sorts, index-friendly|scales to large tables|the default for lists
emerald|Multi-field|~Tie-breakers|Sort.by(a).and(Sort.by(b))|ORDER BY a, b|stable ordering
violet|Direction + case|~Control output|Sort.by(...).descending()|ignoreCase() = LOWER()|newest-first, A-Z

sections.title: findAll() vs findAll(Sort)
sections.content:
| Aspect | `findAll()` | `findAll(Sort)` |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL** | `SELECT * FROM t` | `SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY field` |
| **Order** | DB-dependent | Explicit, by your fields |
| **Where sorting happens** | In Java (if at all) | In the database |
| **Memory** | Loads all, sorts in RAM | DB sorts before sending |
| **Scales** | Poorly for large tables | Well, with an index |

Rule of thumb: never load everything and sort in Java.

sections.title: Wrong — Load Everything, Sort in Java
Right — Let the Database Sort
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **`findAll()`** only when order genuinely doesn't matter or the table is tiny. Use **`findAll(Sort.by(...))`** whenever users see an ordered list (customers A-Z, products by price). Use **chained `Sort`** for tie-breakers, **`Sort.Direction.DESC`** for newest-first feeds, and **`PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)`** for any list that can grow past ~50 items. Never `findAll()` then sort with streams in production.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sorting in Java** — `findAll().stream().sorted(...)` loads the entire table into memory and collapses at scale.
- **Unstable order** — relying on `findAll()` to return insertion order; without `ORDER BY` it isn't guaranteed.
- **No index** — sorting on an unindexed column forces a full scan and sort every call.
- **Forgetting tie-breakers** — single-field sorts can shift page boundaries; chain a second field for stable ordering.

followup_questions: How do you sort by multiple fields in Spring Data?
Can you accept Sort parameters from a REST request in Spring Boot?

seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is the difference between findAll() and findAll(Sort) in JpaRepository? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Sorting a big result set in Java with streams is a scaling trap. It's far better to push the order into the database.
speakable_v2.standard_example: An OrderRepository sorted with Sort.by createdAt

beats.text: Both fetch all rows. Plain findAll returns them in whatever order the database picks. findAll with a Sort adds an order by clause, so the database returns the rows already sorted.
Use plain findAll only for tiny or unordered data. Reach for findAll with Sort whenever users see an ordered list. Chain sorts for tie-breakers, and you'll want an index on any column you sort on.
Sort.by name turns into order by name in SQL. The gotcha is calling findAll first and sorting in Java, which loads the whole table into memory before it sorts.

speakable_v2.cap: So let the database sort, and never pull the whole table into Java to sort it yourself.

questions.question: How does pagination work with JpaRepository?
questions.title: Pagination with JpaRepository and Pageable
questions.direct_answer: A Pageable carries a zero-based page number, size, and optional Sort. A Page contains content plus total counts and therefore normally needs a count query; Spring Data may avoid that query when it can infer the total. A Slice reports only whether another slice exists and usually fetches one extra row instead of counting all matches. The provider renders database-specific limiting SQL, not always literal LIMIT/OFFSET.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can paginate large datasets correctly and know Page runs an extra count query while Slice does not
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting pages are zero-indexed, and using Page everywhere when Slice avoids a costly count query on huge tables
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Page vs Slice, capping max page size, passing a stable Sort, and that PageRequest maps to LIMIT/OFFSET

sections.title: Pagination with Pageable, Page, and Slice
sections.content:
Offset paging asks the database to skip earlier rows, so deep pages can become expensive and concurrent inserts can shift results. Keyset pagination uses the last seen sort values instead, such as createdAt and id, and asks for rows after that cursor.

Whichever method is used, ordering must be complete and deterministic. Pagination without ORDER BY may repeat or omit rows across requests because the database is free to change result order.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: PageRequest page numbers start at zero.
Page adds totalElements/totalPages and normally costs a count query.
Slice avoids total-count metadata and can be cheaper.
Use a deterministic order; large offsets may favor keyset pagination.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending().and(Sort.by("id").descending())) requests the first twenty rows in stable order. A Page is useful when the UI needs 'page 2 of 47'. A Slice is better for 'load more' because it only needs content and hasNext. With a complex join, provide an accurate countQuery when Spring cannot derive one safely. Do not expose unbounded page sizes from client input.

For example, findByStatus(OPEN, PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending())) requests the first 20 open orders. Page also runs or derives a count query; Slice avoids the total count when the UI only needs to know whether another page exists.

sections.title: Pagination at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pageable|~The request|PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)|page is zero-indexed|describes the slice you want
blue|Page<T>|~Slice + metadata|total elements + pages|runs a count query|for numbered pagination UIs
emerald|Slice<T>|~Slice + hasNext|no count query|cheaper on huge tables|for infinite scroll
violet|SQL|~LIMIT/OFFSET|OFFSET = page * size|LIMIT = size|database does the slicing

sections.title: Paginated, Sorted REST Endpoint
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Page where Slice fits** — on million-row tables the count query can take seconds; infinite-scroll UIs don't need totals, so use `Slice`.
- **Off-by-one pages** — pages are **zero-indexed**; if the frontend sends 1-based numbers, subtract 1.
- **No max page size** — a request for `size=1000000` can overwhelm the DB; cap it (e.g., 100).
- **Forgetting sort** — without a stable `Sort`, page boundaries can shift between requests.

followup_questions: What is the difference between Page and Slice in Spring Data?
How do you create a PageRequest with sorting?

seo.metaTitle: Pagination with JpaRepository and Pageable — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How does pagination work with JpaRepository? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Page quietly fires a second count query. On a million-row table, that's exactly where your endpoint slows down.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A paginated orders endpoint returning a Page of orders

beats.text: Pagination means fetching rows in small chunks called pages instead of all at once. You pass a Pageable to a repository method. PageRequest.of with a page number and size builds it, and you get back a Page.
A big table can hold millions of rows. Calling findAll would load them all and can crash the app. Pagination keeps memory steady by reading one page at a time.

items: Pageable describes the slice you want, and pages start at zero.
Page gives you the rows plus totals, like total elements and total pages.
Slice gives you the rows plus a hasNext flag, and it skips the count query.

beats.text: Say you request page two with size twenty. Spring turns that into limit twenty offset forty, so the database returns just those rows. Here's the non-obvious part. Page also runs a second count query for the total, and on a huge table that count is what slows things down.

items: Using Page everywhere when Slice would skip that costly count query.
Forgetting pages start at zero, or never capping the maximum page size.

speakable_v2.cap: So Pageable describes the slice, Page adds totals, and Slice stays light for endless scroll.
followup_handoff: Can you explain Page versus Slice?
How do you add sorting to a page request?

questions.question: What is @Query in Spring Data JPA and when do you use it?
questions.title: @Query Annotation in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: @Query defines JPQL by default and native SQL when nativeQuery=true. Use it when an explicit query communicates the required projection, join, aggregation, fetch plan, or predicate more clearly than method-name derivation. Bind values as parameters. There is no meaningful universal method-name length threshold at which @Query becomes required.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you choose JPQL over native by default and know the @Modifying + @Transactional requirement for writes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for native SQL when JPQL works (losing portability), or omitting @Modifying on UPDATE/DELETE and getting a runtime exception
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @Modifying(clearAutomatically=true) to refresh the persistence context after a bulk update, and DTO projections via JPQL constructor expressions

sections.title: When to Use @Query in a JPA Repository
sections.content:
Derived queries remain excellent for concise lookups. JPQL stays portable at the mapping level, while native SQL enables database-specific features at the cost of portability and often separate count-query work for pagination. A fetch join can prevent a particular lazy-load pattern but collection fetching, duplicate rows, and pagination still need verification.

**Example.** A JPQL grouped projection can return totals by customer, while a bulk @Modifying update changes rows directly and may require clearing stale managed state.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: JPQL names entities and mapped attributes; native SQL names database objects.
Use @Modifying for bulk UPDATE or DELETE repository queries.
Provide a transaction around modifying work and account for stale managed entities.
clearAutomatically is optional; use it only when clearing the entire persistence context is acceptable.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, @Query("select new com.example.OrderTotal(o.customer.id,sum(o.total)) from Order o group by o.customer.id") can return a projection. A bulk status update needs @Modifying and a transaction. Setting clearAutomatically=true avoids stale entities afterward but also detaches unrelated managed changes, so flush/clear behavior must be chosen deliberately.

sections.title: @Query at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|JPQL (default)|~Queries entities|portable across databases|fields validated|use this first
blue|Native SQL|~nativeQuery = true|tables and columns|vendor features (JSONB)|escape hatch only
emerald|@Param|~Named binding|:email in query|@Param("email")|safe, readable
violet|@Modifying|~For writes|UPDATE / DELETE|needs @Transactional|clearAutomatically avoids stale cache

sections.title: Wrong — UPDATE Without @Modifying
Right — @Modifying + @Transactional
JPQL, Native, and Projections
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Native SQL by default** — loses portability and field validation; use JPQL first.
- **Missing `@Modifying`** on UPDATE/DELETE — runtime exception; `@Query` expects SELECT otherwise.
- **No transaction** — even with `@Modifying`, the write needs a `@Transactional` boundary.
- **Stale cache after bulk update** — without `clearAutomatically = true`, the next read may return old cached entities.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Query with JPQL and nativeQuery=true?
What is @Modifying and when do you need it?
How do you return a projection (subset of fields) with @Query?

seo.metaTitle: @Query Annotation in Spring Data JPA — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for What is @Query in Spring Data JPA and when do you use it? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: Write an update inside a Query annotation without Modifying, and Spring throws. It assumed you meant a select.
speakable_v2.standard_example: A repository method with @Query JPQL plus @Modifying for an update

beats.text: The Query annotation lets you write a custom query right on a repository method. It uses JPQL by default, which queries your entity classes. Add nativeQuery true and it runs raw SQL instead. You bind values with named parameters.

Derived method names work great for simple lookups. But stack four or five conditions and the name gets unreadable fast. The Query annotation lets you spell out the exact query, joins and aggregations included.

items: JPQL queries entities and stays portable across databases.
Native SQL unlocks vendor features like PostgreSQL ILIKE or window functions.
Update and delete queries need Modifying plus a transaction, or Spring throws.

beats.text: Say you write an update that sets an order status. Mark it with Modifying and run it in a transaction. Here's the non-obvious part. A bulk update can leave stale entities in the persistence context. Setting clearAutomatically true clears it, so the next read reloads fresh data.

items: Reaching for native SQL when JPQL would do, losing portability.
Leaving off Modifying on an update or delete, which throws at runtime.

speakable_v2.cap: So default to JPQL, keep native SQL for vendor tricks, and don't ship a write without Modifying.
followup_handoff: Can you explain JPQL versus native SQL?

questions.question: How do you add custom implementation to a Spring Data JPA repository?
questions.title: Custom Repository Implementation in Spring Data JPA
questions.direct_answer: Add custom repository behavior with a fragment interface and an implementation discovered by the configured repository-implementation postfix, which defaults to Impl. The main repository extends the fragment interface, and Spring composes the generated repository with that fragment. The recommended fragment model is different from the older pattern of naming one custom class after the whole repository interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the fragment/Impl-suffix pattern for logic beyond derived methods and @Query
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Breaking the exact Impl naming convention or trying to add a method body to the repository interface itself
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Impl suffix is configurable (repositoryImplementationPostfix) and that the Criteria API fits dynamic, optional-filter searches

sections.title: Spring Data Repository Fragments
sections.content: Fragments can be reused by several repositories and composed in declaration order. A manually declared bean name can resolve ambiguous implementations. If a method is suitable for a derived query, specification, Querydsl, or @Query, a custom fragment may be unnecessary; use it for behavior that needs a real implementation boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Define a small fragment interface around related custom operations.
Implement it with the default Impl postfix or configure another postfix.
Extend the fragment from the main repository interface.
Inject EntityManager/JdbcTemplate normally and give the implementation an unambiguous bean identity.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For example, OrderSearch defines search(OrderFilter filter), OrderSearchImpl implements it with EntityManager, and OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, OrderSearch. The default postfix makes OrderSearchImpl the fragment implementation. If repositoryImplementationPostfix is changed, the class name must follow that configuration instead of a universal hard-coded Impl rule.

sections.title: Fragment Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Custom interface|~Declares the method|OrderRepositoryCustom|no body here|the contract
blue|Impl class|~Holds the logic|OrderRepositoryCustomImpl|injects EntityManager|exact Impl suffix
emerald|Main repository|~Extends both|JpaRepository + Custom|one proxy at runtime|generated + custom together
violet|Use cases|~When to do this|dynamic Criteria queries|batch / stored procs|3rd-party integration

sections.title: Step-by-Step Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | What to do | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Define `OrderRepositoryCustom` with the method signature | The contract for custom logic |
| 2 | Implement `OrderRepositoryCustomImpl` (exact `Impl` suffix), inject `EntityManager` | Spring discovers it by name |
| 3 | `OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, OrderRepositoryCustom` | Combines both fragments |
| 4 | Call the custom method on the normal repository bean | Spring's proxy routes it |

The `Impl` suffix is configurable via `@EnableJpaRepositories(repositoryImplementationPostfix = "...")`.

sections.title: Dynamic Filter Query with Criteria API
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Wrong name** — the class must be `<CustomInterface>Impl` exactly; `...Implementation` won't be found.
- **Adding a body to the repository interface** — interfaces can't hold logic; that's what the fragment is for.
- **Injecting the main repository into the Impl** — risks a circular dependency; use `EntityManager`.
- **Reinventing dynamic queries** — for many optional filters, Spring Data **Specifications** or **QueryDSL** may be cleaner than hand-written Criteria.

followup_questions: What is the naming convention for custom repository implementation classes?
When would you use EntityManager directly over @Query?
What is Querydsl and how does it integrate with Spring Data?

seo.metaTitle: Custom Repository Implementation in Spring Data JPA — java backend interview question | InterviewExplainer
seo.metaDescription: Interview answer for How do you add custom implementation to a Spring Data JPA repository? with a clear explanation, practical example, common mistakes, and follow-up questions.

speakable_v2.hook: With the default repository-fragment postfix, OrderSearchImpl matches the OrderSearch fragment; a configured postfix changes that convention.
speakable_v2.standard_example: An OrderRepository plus OrderRepositoryCustom and OrderRepositoryCustomImpl

beats.text: Custom implementation uses the fragment pattern. You write a small interface for the method, then an implementation class whose name ends in Impl. That class injects the EntityManager. Your main repository extends both JpaRepository and the custom interface.

The Impl class holds the logic and injects the EntityManager.
The main repository extends both, and Spring builds one proxy from the pieces.

beats.text: Picture a search form where users pick any mix of filters. You build the where clause with the Criteria builder, adding a predicate only when a filter is set. Here's the non-obvious part. By default the fragment implementation follows the fragment interface name plus Impl; the postfix can be configured.

items: Breaking the exact Impl name, so Spring can't find the class.
Injecting the main repository into the Impl, which creates a circular dependency.

speakable_v2.cap: So use an interface, an Impl class, and a main repository that extends both.

questions.question: What is @Transactional on a Spring Data JPA repository method?
questions.title: @Transactional on Spring Data JPA Methods
questions.direct_answer: Spring Data's inherited CRUD methods already have transaction settings: reads are commonly read-only and writes use a regular transaction. Put @Transactional on a service method when several repository operations form one unit of work. readOnly=true is a hint and optimization opportunity, not a portable guarantee that dirty checking is skipped or writes are impossible. Proxy and rollback rules still apply.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you place transactions at the service layer for atomicity and understand Spring's proxy-based behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting @Transactional on repository interfaces (redundant) or calling a @Transactional method from the same class (proxy bypassed, no transaction)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain readOnly=true skipping dirty checking and that checked exceptions don't roll back by default

sections.title: Transaction Boundaries Around Spring Data Repositories
Quick revision
content: Use a service transaction to make a multi-repository use case atomic.
Declared query methods do not automatically inherit every CRUD method's transaction setting.
readOnly is a hint whose effect depends on the transaction manager/provider.
Self-invocation and default rollback rules are the same as other proxy-based @Transactional uses.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A transfer that debits one account and credits another belongs in one @Transactional service method. Calling each repository method separately without an outer transaction can create separate boundaries and allow a partial result. Spring Data supplies defaults for methods inherited from SimpleJpaRepository, but a custom query method may need an explicit transaction when its behavior requires one. For modifying @Query methods, use @Modifying and a transaction. readOnly=true can tune flush behavior, but the database and provider decide the exact enforcement.

sections.title: @Transactional at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Where it belongs|~Service layer|orchestrates repos|business atomicity|not on controllers
blue|Default rollback|~RuntimeException|auto rollback|checked = no rollback|use rollbackFor for checked
emerald|readOnly = true|~For queries|skips dirty checking|faster reads|signals intent
violet|Proxy limit|~Self-invocation|same-class call bypasses proxy|no transaction starts|call from another bean

sections.title: Wrong — Self-Invocation Skips the Transaction
Right — Transaction at the Public Entry Point
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`@Transactional` on repository interfaces** — redundant; writes are already transactional. It belongs on service methods.
- **Skipping `readOnly = true`** on read-only services — Hibernate needlessly tracks entities for changes.
- **Self-invocation** — calling a `@Transactional` method from another method in the **same class** bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts.
- **Expecting checked exceptions to roll back** — only `RuntimeException`/`Error` roll back by default; use `rollbackFor = Exception.class` for checked ones.

beats.text: The Transactional annotation runs a method inside one database transaction. Everything commits together or rolls back together. Repository writes are already transactional, so you put this on service methods that call several repositories.

Often several writes have to succeed as one unit. Picture a checkout that lowers stock and saves an order. If the save fails, you don't want the stock change to stick. One transaction makes both happen or neither.

items: Put it on service methods that span several repositories, so they stay atomic.
Use readOnly true on query methods to skip dirty checking.
By default only runtime exceptions roll back, so checked ones need rollbackFor.

beats.text: In a checkout, lowering stock and saving the order share one transaction. If stock runs short, the whole thing rolls back. Here's the non-obvious part. Calling your own Transactional method from inside the same class skips the proxy, so no transaction even starts.

items: Calling a Transactional method from the same class, which bypasses the proxy.
Expecting checked exceptions to roll back, when only runtime ones do.

speakable_v2.cap: So keep transactions at the service layer, where a self call won't quietly skip the proxy.
